messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Updates to biogeographical stochastic mapping
parts:
Hi all,

I've posted some updates to the stochastic mapping code at PhyloWiki. (Source the code the same as before.)

Some users were having difficulties with large trees and state spaces -- basically, some branches were failing to simulate successfully even after many many tries.  This is not unexpected: e.g. the Huelsenbeck et al. 2003 paper notes that stochastic mapping will be efficient for small state spaces, but increasingly less so for large state spaces.

After investigating the issue on this dataset (800+ species, ~10 areas, most species narrow but a few widespread), I found:

1. The fundamentals work

2. The problem is just that the models being used just don't fit the data very well

3. In particular, the hard branches to simulate are e.g. tips that are very widespread, when most relatives are narrow ranges.  Under DEC or DEC+J (you may find DIVALIKE or BAYAREALIKE-type models are better, or some new model that combines some of their features), if you have a branch with the bottom state=A and the top state=ACEDFGI, this requires just the right combination of range-addition events to get to ACEDFGI.  If widespread tip ranges are rare, then the ML d was estimated to be low, and thus it takes a whole bunch of "lucky" events on the same branch to get the branch simulated correctly.

I tried maxtries=10^8 tries and still some branches were failing to simulate.


The only fixes would be to:

(a) put NAs for those branches, thus biasing event counts etc., and requiring a bunch of code to deal with NAs

(b) do some hack to force a successful history for those branches.

I chose (b).  Basically, if a branch fails to simulate a successful history before the max number of tries, the function now does a manual history that determines the required range gain/range loss events and puts them in a random order on the branch, with a uniform random distribution on timing (and excluding any histories with a null range intermediate).

Actually, this is likely to be basically as good as what you would get if you did trillions of simulations to get one success -- because the required events are ultra-rare anyway, conditional on a history which occurred despite the improbability, the timing of these very improbable events should be approximately uniform random.

The script will print various warnings to screen when (b) happens.  If you see too many of those, feel free to increase maxtries to e.g. 10^6 or 10^7 or higher.  You will then be able to decide what tradeoff works for you regarding timing (lower maxtries will be faster) vs. "perfection". 


4. I also added multicore processing for get_inputs_for_stochastic_mapping(), which gets slow for large state spaces and trees.  I added this to the stochastic mapping example script:

===================
#######################################################
# Get the inputs for Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping
# Note: this can be slow for large state spaces and trees, since 
# the independent likelihoods for each branch are being pre-calculated
# E.g., for 10 areas, this requires calculation of a 1024x1024 matrix
# for each branch.  On a tree with ~800 tips and thus ~1600 branches, this was about 1.6 gigs
# for storage of "BSM_inputs_file.Rdata".
# Update: 2015-09-23 -- now, if you used multicore functionality for the ML analysis,
# the same settings will be used for get_inputs_for_stochastic_mapping().
#######################################################
BSM_inputs_fn = "BSM_inputs_file.Rdata"
runInputsSlow = TRUE
if (runInputsSlow)
    {
    stochastic_mapping_inputs_list = get_inputs_for_stochastic_mapping(res=res)
    save(stochastic_mapping_inputs_list, file=BSM_inputs_fn)
    } else {
    # Loads to "stochastic_mapping_inputs_list"
    load(BSM_inputs_fn)
    } # END if (runInputsSlow)

===================


Cheers,
Nick
